name: Uma Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the Harlow estate, have done for nineteen years. It's a big place, 400 hectares, about 250 beef cattle and a lot of potatoes. I'm the stock person, so I check the cattle first thing, sort feed, move groups between fields, and in autumn I'm on the potato harvester like everyone else. The family who own it are decent enough. Mr Harlow's son runs it now and he's keener on figures than his father was.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The potato harvest, every year. Twelve-hour days in the dust for six weeks. My partner Tom drives a delivery van for the builders' merchant, and with Elsa at fourteen and Finn at ten, somebody's always needing a lift somewhere. I don't touch any of that AI stuff. I've got enough on with the phone the estate gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years there's something that's going to change farming forever and mostly it doesn't. I'd say it in the tea room and that's about it, I don't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things stay as they are, and that's fine by me. I know my job, I know my cattle, and I've got a steady wage. If young Mr Harlow buys some clever software for the office, that's his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. We'd keep putting a bit by each month, about 100, and keep chipping at the mortgage. Maybe this would be the year I finally fix the fence at the bottom of our own garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the tools if the estate brought them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd learn the bit I needed and no more. I watched the office manager spend a whole morning arguing with a computer about a cattle passport. I could have done it with a pen in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the estate who'd want things to change more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Mr Harlow, probably. He's always at shows looking at shiny machines. But he's also careful with money, so I don't think he'd buy anything that didn't pay for itself.

S0.say: I'm not surprised. Every few years there's something that's going to change farming forever, and mostly it doesn't.
S0.think: It means things stay as they are, and that's fine by me. I know my job and my cattle and I've got a steady wage.
S0.do: Carries on as she is, putting about 100 a month aside and chipping away at the mortgage. Might finally fix the fence at the bottom of the family garden.
S0.quote: I watched the office manager spend a whole morning arguing with a computer about a cattle passport.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is comfortable with routine and quietly sceptical of new technology. She doesn't blame or praise anyone, describing the estate owners as decent and careful. She'd learn only what she was made to learn.

steps.text: Keep checking, feeding and moving the Harlow estate's 250 beef cattle as always
Finally fix the fence at the bottom of the family's garden
Keep putting about 100 a month by and chipping at the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mm. That one I'd believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, there's always change and you get on with it. No point getting worked up about it in front of people. I'd probably say that to the other workers at the estate as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. Young Mr Harlow has already been looking at GPS collars that move the cattle without anyone walking them. If he buys those, half of what I do goes, and he doesn't need two stock people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well, and I'd wait and see what the estate actually buys. We'd save a bit more, maybe 150 a month instead of 100. I suppose I'd ask around the other farms quietly, just to know what's out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A sort of nagging feeling when I'm out with the cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the other stock person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren. He's 31 and good with his phone. If the estate only keeps one stock person, I think they'd keep the younger one who'll learn the GPS collars. I don't blame them, I'd probably do the same in their place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get on with it, but you'd also be asking around other farms. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. You say one thing in the tea room and you do another thing at home. Tom would tell you I've been worrying about jobs since the day I started.

S1.say: It's how things go. There's always change and you get on with it, and there's no point getting worked up about it in front of people.
S1.think: Young Mr Harlow has been looking at GPS collars that move cattle without anyone walking them. If he buys those, half my job goes and he won't need two stock people.
S1.do: Keeps her head down, does her job well and waits to see what the estate buys. Raises savings from 100 to 150 a month and quietly asks around other farms about work.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a nagging feeling while out with the cattle.
S1.quote: If the estate only keeps one stock person, I think they'd keep the younger one who'll learn the GPS collars.
S1.fieldNote: Uma's public calm hides a specific fear: GPS cattle collars and a younger colleague. She refuses to blame her employer and sees it as plain business. She admits openly to saying one thing in the tea room and another at home.

steps.text: Wait to see whether the estate buys GPS collars that move the cattle
Raise the family savings from 100 to 150 a month
Quietly ask around the other farms about stock work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office goes first and the field after. That's three years, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the tea room I'd say the cattle still need a person for now, and the robots are three years off, so no point panicking. I'd say it to Darren and the lads on the harvester. I wouldn't say anything else, I don't go on about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the first thing that goes in 2028 is the office, and the office is where young Mr Harlow does his sums. A computer that plans the grazing better than me tells him exactly how few people he needs, and he'd have the numbers ready for when the robots come in 2031. Tom's van is the same, someone has to carry the timber for now, and then nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away, no holiday, and Elsa's school trip to the coast would have to go. We'd put about 250 a month on the mortgage so it's smaller by 2031. I'd ask young Mr Harlow straight out whether there's a job for me after the robots, which I've never done in nineteen years. I'd let Tom look for something steadier first, because his van goes at the same time as my cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. I'd lie awake doing sums, and the three years would feel like a countdown, not a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Elsa about the school trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, that money's tight and it might get tighter. My daughter would be upset for a day about the school trip, and then she'd tell me it didn't matter, which would be worse. She's fourteen, she'd understand more than I'd want her to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Mr Harlow straight out. What do you think he'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He’d say something like ‘let’s see how it goes, Uma’, which means no. He’s not a bad man. Young Mr Harlow would already have the computer’s figures on how few stock people the estate needs in a folder on his desk.

S2.say: The cattle still need a person for now, and the robots are three years off, so there's no point panicking. That's all I'd say in the tea room.
S2.think: The first thing that goes in 2028 is the estate office, and a computer that plans grazing better than me tells young Mr Harlow how few people he needs once the robots come in 2031. Tom's delivery van is on the same clock.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, dropping the holiday and Elsa's school trip, and puts about 250 a month on the mortgage before 2031. Asks young Mr Harlow directly about a job after the robots, and lets Tom look for steadier work first.
S2.feel: Sick with worry. She'd lie awake doing sums, and the three years would feel like a countdown, not a cushion.
S2.quote: Young Mr Harlow would already have the computer’s figures on how few stock people the estate needs in a folder on his desk.
S2.fieldNote: Uma read the three-year gap as a countdown rather than a breathing space. She expects the estate's planning to go to AI first and to be used to decide who stays when the robots come. For the first time in nineteen years she'd ask the owner directly about her future, and she already expects the answer to be no.

steps.text: Cancel the family holiday and Elsa's school trip to the coast
Put about 250 a month on the mortgage before the robots come in 2031
Let Tom look for steadier work than the van first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the office, eight for the field. I'd be 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, there's always change and you get on with it. If people at the estate asked, I'd tell them there's eight years before a robot can move a herd. That's a long time in farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same ending, just with more time to watch it coming. I'd be 51 when the robots arrive, Elsa would be grown and Finn nearly. I think I'd spend five years watching the estate office change and three more waiting for the field to follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd save as hard as we can, about 200 a month, and I'd sell the second car when it needs its next big repair. I'd wait and see what the estate actually buys in 2031 before doing anything else. I'd make sure Elsa takes her exams seriously, because I want her to have more choices than I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slowly. It's like a bad tooth you know you'll have to deal with one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the new machines this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estate paid for it and gave me the time, maybe. I'm not going to the college in the evenings at fifty to sit with teenagers. I know that's stubborn, Tom tells me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Elsa to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where people need people. Nursing, maybe, or the vet's. I'd like my daughter to have a job where somebody's glad to see her come through the door.

S3.say: There's always change and you get on with it. There's eight years before a robot can move a herd, and that's a long time in farming.
S3.think: It's the same ending with more time to watch it coming, and I'd be 51 when the robots arrive. I'd spend five years watching the estate office change and three more waiting for the field to follow.
S3.do: Saves about 200 a month and plans to sell the second car at its next big repair. Waits to see what the estate buys in 2031 before acting, and makes sure Elsa takes her exams seriously.
S3.feel: Anxious, but slowly, like a bad tooth she knows she'll have to deal with one day.
S3.quote: I'd like my daughter to have a job where somebody's glad to see her come through the door.
S3.fieldNote: Uma still won't retrain unless the estate pays and gives her the time, and she owns that stubbornness. The extra years mostly let her save and get her children through school. Her hopes for her daughter are about being needed by people rather than about money.

steps.text: Save about 200 a month and sell the second car at its next repair
Wait to see what machines the Harlow estate buys in 2031
Make sure Elsa takes her exams seriously

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039 for the robots. Finn would be twenty-three. That's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anything can happen. People said the same about the milking machines once. In the tea room I'd probably just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 56 by the time a robot could do my job, and the children would be grown. That's not retirement, but it's not starting out either. The office would change from 2036 and I wouldn't miss the paperwork one bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the cattle and keep putting 150 a month by, and pay the mortgage down when I can. I'd steer Elsa and Finn towards something solid. I wouldn't learn anything new unless the estate asked me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, now and then. Mostly I'd be thinking about the kids, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by something solid for the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to say a trade, plumbing or electrics. But if robots can do hands-on work by 2039, even that's not certain. If even a trade isn't safe, I don't really know what to tell my kids, and that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Biscuit, your cow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Biscuit would be long gone by then, she's twelve already. That's a strange thought, that my favourite cow won't live to see it.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and anything can happen. People said the same about the milking machines once.
S4.think: I'd be 56 by the time a robot could do my job, with the children grown, which isn't retirement but isn't starting out either. The office paperwork changing from 2036 is something I wouldn't miss.
S4.do: Carries on with the cattle, keeps putting 150 a month by and pays the mortgage down when she can. Steers Elsa and Finn towards solid work and doesn't learn anything new unless the estate asks.
S4.feel: Uneasy now and then, mostly about the children rather than herself.
S4.quote: If even a trade isn't safe, I don't really know what to tell my kids, and that's the honest answer.
S4.fieldNote: With thirteen years before robots, Uma's worry moves almost entirely onto her children. Her old advice to learn a trade no longer works in this picture, and she admits she has nothing to replace it. She'd keep working as she is without retraining.

steps.text: Keep looking after the Harlow estate's beef cattle as she does now
Keep putting 150 a month by and pay the mortgage down
Steer Elsa and Finn towards work that will still need people

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tom's van and my cattle would both go to the robots by 2031, and three years isn't long enough for someone like me to find somewhere to go. What would help is money from the government to tide families over, quickly, and someone telling me plainly what jobs there'd be for someone like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the cattle would think. I know that sounds daft. But I've got a cow called Biscuit who follows me round the field, and no collar's going to get that.

headlineQuote: I've got a cow called Biscuit who follows me round the field, and no collar's going to get that.
portrait: Uma Jensen, 43, has been the stock person on the large Harlow estate for nineteen years, working with beef cattle and potatoes. She never uses AI and prefers to keep her head down, treating change as plain business. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy about GPS collars and a younger colleague under steady change. Fast AGI alarms her because the estate's planning goes to AI in 2028 and both her job and her partner's van job would follow by 2031, so she'd cut spending and pay down the mortgage. With more time she still won't retrain, and her worry moves to her children, for whom even a trade no longer feels safe.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her partner would both lose their hands-on jobs to robots by 2031 with too little time to find other work.
whatWouldHelp: Quick government money to tide families over, and someone telling her plainly what work would exist for someone like her.
